cells.tense: Right now you're the one tending what's growing, and you're holding two needs at once without dropping either.
cells.ask: Let one of the two things you're holding this week finish before you pick up the next, and notice what loosens when it's done.
cells.core:
You're tending what's growing, and you're doing it with care rather than control. Two people, two needs, sometimes pulling opposite ways — and you're not forcing either one. You've found the pace where attention keeps both alive without exhausting you, and the people around you can feel the difference between being managed and being kept.

When something you've been tending reaches the end of what it needed, letting it go comes easily. It doesn't feel like defeat. It feels like the whole point. That ease is what frees you to turn toward the next thing still growing — and the acknowledgment you haven't asked for yet is safe to ask for now.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending both, holding them steady, and it's working.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: in the part of your life where you stay in contact with people — feeling with them, not just about them

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead you're bracing for how this turns out, and it hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Let one picture of how a relationship should end come out of you — say it to someone — instead of managing it before it's real.
cells.core:
You're tending what's growing, but you're tending a future version of it. You've imagined how the conversation goes, what they'll need before they ask, what the ending looks like — and the care has turned into managing what hasn't arrived. The holding has become clutching.

What you're actually reaching for is completion — the deep satisfaction of having fully felt and fully lived something through. That comes from imagining out of what's already happened, not what might. Let one future version of a relationship go by saying it out loud to the person. The energy that's been bracing gets somewhere real to land.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding a relationship that hasn't happened yet.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, responsible care

cells.tense: You stopped, and you're still standing where you stopped.
cells.ask: Tell one person one specific thing about what you've been building or tending — the part you'd normally keep to yourself — and let the ordinary reply arrive.
cells.core:
You're tending what's growing, but you've gone quiet about it. The care is still happening — you show up, you do the thing — but you've stopped arriving in the room where anyone can see the tending. There's a distance between you and the people you're caring for, and you're on the far side of it.

What's waiting on the other edge isn't a push to feel more or a push to try harder. It's continuation — the reason you kept at this in the first place is still underneath everything. Say one thing about what you've been building to one person. The ordinary reply tells you it's still worth something, and the current moves when you move.
cells.sheetLine: You're still tending it. You've just stopped showing anyone.

cells.tense: You're already tending this, and you're describing it as if it were happening on its own.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, to the person who benefits most from what you tend: this is yours to claim — this was built by these hands, and here is what it cost to keep it growing.
cells.core:
You're tending what's growing — you pick what to keep alive and you keep it alive — but you've been calling it upkeep, or logistics, or just what needed doing. The care keeps moving under its own weight; the saying-so never happened. Somewhere along the way the hand came off the work.

What you're doing is the same care as finishing something and letting it go with hands open. That kind of release only comes from completion — from saying the thing is done and it was made by these hands. Say what you tend is yours, to one person, in plain words. The same act, owned instead of unnamed.
